editorial.title: LiteLLM investigation traces stolen CI access eleven days before poisoned release
editorial.summary: LiteLLM’s investigation connects an October 10 secret-stealing workflow to the October 21 publication of compromised litellm==1.107.0 artifacts. Socket independently found traces of the earlier workflow. The maintainer says token hashes link a stolen maintainer credential to approval of the later release.
editorial.why_it_matters: The revised timeline shows why reviewing only the final package upload can miss the earlier breach of the release boundary. Repository credentials, workflow execution and publishing approvals all belong in the same investigation, while downstream exposure still depends on whether affected artifacts ran.
editorial.action: Review October repository and CI activity as well as installations of the affected PyPI and container artifacts. Preserve logs, identify credentials available to the compromised workflows and affected processes, rotate exposed tokens from a trusted environment, and rebuild from verified clean artifacts.

sections.heading: The newly documented lead-up
paragraphs: LiteLLM reports that an attacker reached its experimental Agent Platform on October 10 and extracted a GitHub CLI OAuth token associated with an organization owner. With that authority, a throwaway workflow in the main repository posted CI secrets to an attacker-controlled endpoint. Socket separately recovered evidence that the secret-stealing workflow ran on October 10, eleven days before the poisoned release.

The maintainer says the audit-log hash of the stolen GH_TOKEN matches the token used for approval at the later production release gate. This is stronger linkage than the earlier public timeline alone could establish. The revised account attributes that link to LiteLLM’s investigation rather than treating all preceding activity as independently observed by Socket.

sections.heading: From repository authority to release artifact
paragraphs: LiteLLM says the attacker changed the release workflow to take source from a fork. The same investigation reports that a compromised litellm==1.107.0 was published to PyPI and container registries on October 21. Microsoft’s artifact analysis describes files that Python can execute during normal interpreter initialization, so the execution boundary is wider than an explicit LiteLLM import.

The build and approval steps explain how expected distribution channels could carry attacker-controlled content. They do not prove that every downstream environment installed the artifact, executed the startup files or lost credentials. Each deployment needs its own artifact and execution check.

sections.heading: How to use this correction
paragraphs: The previous edition covered the poisoned release and credential risk. This revision adds the earlier credential-theft sequence and the maintainer’s evidence connecting it to release approval. It does not describe a separate LiteLLM incident or alter the original publication record.

Investigate affected artifacts and CI authority together. Identify package versions and image digests in use, preserve workflow and host evidence, then rotate exposed credentials from a trusted environment. Current maintainer and government guidance should control the detailed response for each deployment.
